paper.title: Boys left behind: The effects of summer camp and follow-up strategies on academic, personal, and social competencies
paper.code_data_availability: Data availability statement (p. 9): 'The authors do not have permission to share data.' The study uses Danish administrative register data available through Statistics Denmark; …

registers.name_in_paper: Danish administrative register data available through Statistics Denmark

registers.role: sample frame / linkage: all educational choices in Denmark; private vs public schooling, school and classroom movements, special needs teaching, and which grade a boy attends

registers.name_in_paper: average assessment mark and readiness assessment for upper secondary education in grades 8 and 9, obtained from the Ministry of Education
registers.years: 2015-2019 (readiness assessment first conducted in 2015, reformed in 2019)

registers.name_in_paper: information on dyslexia, psychiatric diagnoses, results from national tests in reading and math, school absence, socio-emotional skills, and school well-being
socioeconomic information describing the demographics, employment, income and educational level of the parents
the camp provider's registration of the boys who attended the main summer camp

linkages: Pupils linked over time in an individual-level panel across grades 8 and 9 (and back to grades 5-7 for the placebo tests)
Pupils linked to their parents' demographics, employment, income and educational level
The 241 summer camp participants identified from the camp provider's registration and linked to the Statistics Denmark register data

sample.universe: All grade 8 boys in Danish public and private schooling in the school years 2014/2015 to 2018/2019 (camp cohorts 2015-2019); the full population of pupils in the Danish school system is covered by the register data
selection_rules: Grade 8 boys in the school years 2014/2015 to 2018/2019 are pooled when estimating the overall consequences of summer camp participation
The readiness assessment was first conducted in 2015 and reformed in 2019, which restricts the analysis to this four-year period
Camp participants are the 241 boys who applied, were invited and attended the main camp; boys who were invited but did not show up are not registered by the camp provider and cannot be identified
For the triple differences, camp cohorts 2015-2016 (individual mentoring) are compared with camp cohorts 2017-2019 (group mentoring)
sample.period: Grade 8 school years 2014/2015 to 2018/2019; camp cohorts 2015-2019
sample.n_observations: 277,043 pupil observations in the overall readiness assessment regressions (Table 1 and Table 2 column 2); 479,540 for the average assessment mark in the triple differences (Table 2 column 1); 263,480 / 263,153 / 265,354 for the personal / social / academic readiness assessments
sample.n_individuals: 158,231 boys, of which 241 participated at the summer camp between 2015 and 2019

construction_notes: Each continuous assessment mark is standardized within subject and within the timing of the assessment to mean zero and standard deviation one; the average assessment mark is then standardized again within the timing of the assessment, so coefficients are in standard deviation units
The grading occurs in December and June of grades 8 and 9; the June grade 8 grading was initiated in 2018 and does not exist for previous years
The readiness assessment takes place only in December and is registered once in each of grades 8 and 9
Academic grading in Denmark is on a 7-point scale: 12(A), 10(B), 7(C), 4(D), 02(E), 00(FX), -3(F)
Missing values are imputed with the value zero and a binary indicator is added to the conditioning set
The non-camp/mentoring comparison group is reweighted by Entropy Balancing (Hainmueller, 2012) so that the covariate means are identical to the camp/mentoring group (Table A.1, column 8)
Standard errors are clustered at the individual level following Bertrand et al. (2004)
Approximately 8% of the camp boys left during the two weeks of camp (recorded from 2017 onwards), so the estimates are intention-to-treat effects for those showing up at the first day
Camp boys are on average 1.2 standard deviations below the non-camp boys in the average assessment mark at both grade 8 assessments
The total cost of the summer camp including the follow-up program is approximately 5,000 USD per pupil

claims.statement: Participation in the two-week summer camp with a one-year mentoring follow-up increases the probability that a grade 8 boy is assessed ready for upper secondary education at the December grade 9 readiness assessment (Table 1, column 1: raw difference-in-differences without covariates).

treatment.label: Camp/mentoring participation (two-week summer camp with a one-year follow-up mentoring program)

definition.value: Binary variable Camp_i equal to one for the 241 boys who applied, were invited and attended the main two-week intensive learning camp in the summer holiday between grades 8 and 9 (camp cohorts 2015-2019) together with the mandatory one-year follow-up mentoring program; approximately 8% left during the two weeks, so the estimand is an intention-to-treat effect for those showing up at the first day of camp.

timing.value: Treatment takes place in the summer holiday between grade 8 and grade 9; the mandatory mentoring follow-up program runs for the following year.

outcome.label: Overall readiness assessment for upper secondary education

register_source.value: Educational readiness assessment / average assessment mark obtained from the Ministry of Education and linked to the Danish administrative register data available through Statistics Denmark; no register code or variable name is given.

definition.value: Binary indicator equal to one if the pupil's primary teachers assess him as ready for upper secondary education. The teachers assess the academic, personal and social competencies of the pupil and all three criteria must be met for the pupil to be assessed as ready. The assessment includes all pupils in public and private schooling and takes place only in December; it was first conducted in 2015 and reformed in 2019.

timing.value: Measured at the educational readiness assessment in December of grade 9 (post-period), compared with the December grade 8 assessment (pre-period); the readiness assessment takes place only in December and is registered once in each of grades 8 and 9.

units.value: share of pupils assessed ready for upper secondary education (binary outcome; multiply by 100 to read the coefficient as percentage points)

estimand.target_population: Boys who applied with a parent, were invited and showed up at the first day of the two-week summer camp (camp cohorts 2015-2019)
estimand.time_horizon: At the educational readiness assessment in December of grade 9, i.e. about six months after the summer camp and halfway through the one-year follow-up program
estimand.formal_query: E[Y | do(Camp=1)] - E[Y | do(Camp=0)] for grade 8 boys, as an intention-to-treat contrast for those showing up at the first day of camp

population.description: All grade 8 boys in Danish public and private schooling observed in the school years 2014/2015 to 2018/2019 (camp cohorts 2015-2019): 158,231 boys, of which 241 participated at the summer camp.
population.ages: Pupils in grade 8 and grade 9 of Danish lower secondary education
subgroups_defined: camp cohorts with individual mentoring follow-up (2015-2016)
camp cohorts with group mentoring follow-up (2017-2019)
population.selection: Camp participants are boys who applied together with a parent, were invited and attended the main camp; due to legal issues the camp provider only registered boys who attended the main camp, so boys invited who did not show up are unobserved. The comparison group is the remaining population of grade 8 boys in Danish public and private schooling; the readiness-assessment sample is restricted to pupils observed in the readiness assessment, which was first conducted in 2015 and reformed in 2019.

identification.source_of_variation: Participation in a two-week intensive learning summer camp with a one-year mentoring follow-up in the holiday between grades 8 and 9, compared before (grade 8) and after (grade 9) for participants and non-participants; the comparison group is reweighted by Entropy Balancing.

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: there can be no differential trends between the camp/mentoring and non-camp/mentoring groups in the absence of program participation.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Pre-program trends in the average assessment mark (Fig. 1 shows no difference in effect between December and June of grade 8); placebo test with a randomly selected synthetic 'camp/mentoring' group (Table A.9); a fake camp date in the summer holiday between grades 5 and 6 using national tests in reading and math (Table A.10); placebo tests on absence, socio-emotional skills and school well-being from grade 7 to grade 8 (Tables A.11-A.12).

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: the camp boys do not change their behaviour or performance before the camp in anticipation of participating (behaviour changes prior to summer camp could bias the estimates).
key_assumptions.supported_by: The national reading score in grade 8, measured after application but before the camp, and placebo tests on absence, socio-emotional skills and school well-being from grade 7 to grade 8 (Tables A.10-A.12) show no significant evidence of increased motivation.

implies_edges.to: pre-camp outcomes (grade 7-8 motivation, absence, school well-being, national test scores)

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference: a boy's outcome does not depend on whether other boys participate in the camp/mentoring program (the non-participants are a clean comparison group).

implies_edges.to: a boy's own outcome

threats_discussed: Selection bias: camp/mentoring participating boys comprise a different population compared to the remaining population of boys who do not participate
Differential (non-parallel) trends in school performance between camp and non-camp boys
Camp boys being more motivated to change their behaviour before the camp than non-participants
Teachers grading the boys may be influenced by knowing who participated in the program
Camp boys changing their desired upper secondary education between grades 8 and 9, which lowers the bar for being assessed ready
Applying for the camp may be related to the limitations of the boy's local school
The positive effect might originate from the boys-only teaching rather than from the summer camp itself
robustness_checks: Gradually richer specifications, covariates and individual fixed effects (Table 1; Table A.2)
Entropy balancing on one, two and three moments and propensity score matching with 3, 5 and 10 neighbours (Table A.8)
Alternative comparison groups: boys from schools with camp participants enrolled and schools that never sent pupils to the camp (Table A.7)
Externally censored grade 9 school leaving exams and written exams instead of teacher assessment marks (Figures A.3 and A.4)
Placebo test with a randomly selected fake treatment group (Table A.9)
Fake camp date in the summer holiday between grades 5 and 6 using national tests in reading and math (Table A.10)
Placebo tests on absence, socio-emotional skills and school well-being from grade 7 to grade 8 (Tables A.11-A.12)
Test for effects on changing the desired upper secondary education (Table A.6)

estimator.value: OLS difference-in-differences (linear probability model)

estimation.specification: Eq. (1) with Time_i a binary post indicator (December grade 8 vs December grade 9); the reported coefficient is Camp X Post. Raw difference-in-differences without covariates.
estimation.clustering: Standard errors are clustered on the individual level (Bertrand et al., 2004)

claims.statement: Participation in the two-week summer camp with a one-year mentoring follow-up raises the standardized average assessment mark measured in June of grade 9 (about twelve months after the camp).

treatment.label: Camp/mentoring participation (two-week summer camp with a one-year follow-up mentoring program)

definition.value: Binary variable Camp_i equal to one for the 241 boys who applied, were invited and attended the main two-week intensive learning camp in the summer holiday between grades 8 and 9 (camp cohorts 2015-2019) together with the mandatory one-year follow-up mentoring program; approximately 8% left during the two weeks, so the estimand is an intention-to-treat effect for those showing up at the first day of camp.

timing.value: Treatment takes place in the summer holiday between grade 8 and grade 9; the mandatory mentoring follow-up program runs for the following year.

outcome.label: Average assessment mark (GPA), standardized to mean zero and standard deviation one

register_source.value: Educational readiness assessment / average assessment mark obtained from the Ministry of Education and linked to the Danish administrative register data available through Statistics Denmark; no register code or variable name is given.

definition.value: The average assessment mark is an expression of the pupil's academic level averaged across all subjects the pupil attends, assigned by the teachers against the subjects' academic goals. Each continuous assessment mark is standardized within subject and timing of assessment to mean zero and standard deviation one; the average is then standardized again within the timing of the assessment, so coefficients are in standard deviation units.

timing.value: Measured at the June grade 9 assessment, about twelve months after the summer camp, relative to the December grade 8 assessment (reference time-point).

units.value: standard deviations of the standardized average assessment mark

magnitude.interpretation: Overall, I find effects of 15% of a standard deviation both 6 and 12 months after camp/mentoring participation; participating in the two-week summer camp with a one-year follow-up reduces the learning gap to the full population of boys by 14% and by 40% when compared to boys with similar characteristics.

estimand.target_population: Boys who applied with a parent, were invited and showed up at the first day of the two-week summer camp (camp cohorts 2015-2019)
estimand.time_horizon: Event-study coefficient at the assessment in June of grade 9 (about twelve months after the camp), with December grade 8 as the reference time-point
estimand.formal_query: E[Y | do(Camp=1)] - E[Y | do(Camp=0)] for grade 8 boys, as an intention-to-treat contrast for those showing up at the first day of camp

population.description: Grade 8 boys in Danish public and private schooling with repeated teacher assessment marks across grades 8 and 9, camp cohorts 2015-2019
population.ages: Pupils in grade 8 and grade 9 of Danish lower secondary education
subgroups_defined: camp cohorts with individual mentoring follow-up (2015-2016)
camp cohorts with group mentoring follow-up (2017-2019)
population.selection: Camp participants are boys who applied together with a parent, were invited and attended the main camp; due to legal issues the camp provider only registered boys who attended the main camp, so boys invited who did not show up are unobserved. The comparison group is the remaining population of grade 8 boys in Danish public and private schooling; the readiness-assessment sample is restricted to pupils observed in the readiness assessment, which was first conducted in 2015 and reformed in 2019.

identification.source_of_variation: Participation in a two-week intensive learning summer camp with a one-year mentoring follow-up in the holiday between grades 8 and 9, compared before (grade 8) and after (grade 9) for participants and non-participants; the comparison group is reweighted by Entropy Balancing.

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: there can be no differential trends between the camp/mentoring and non-camp/mentoring groups in the absence of program participation.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Pre-program trends in the average assessment mark (Fig. 1 shows no difference in effect between December and June of grade 8); placebo test with a randomly selected synthetic 'camp/mentoring' group (Table A.9); a fake camp date in the summer holiday between grades 5 and 6 using national tests in reading and math (Table A.10); placebo tests on absence, socio-emotional skills and school well-being from grade 7 to grade 8 (Tables A.11-A.12).

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional parallel trends after reweighting: once the non-camp/mentoring group is reweighted by Entropy Balancing so that the covariate means are identical to the camp/mentoring group, the two groups' outcomes would have evolved in parallel; without it school performance is likely to develop differently with the underlying distribution of covariates.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Column 8 of Table A.1 shows that the means in the camp/mentoring and non-camp/mentoring groups are perfectly balanced across the full set of covariates; alternative balancing methods and propensity score matching (Table A.8) give similar estimates.

key_assumptions.assumption: The reweighted non-camp/mentoring comparison group has common support with the camp/mentoring group over the balanced covariates (positivity of the balancing weights).
No anticipation: the camp boys do not change their behaviour or performance before the camp in anticipation of participating (behaviour changes prior to summer camp could bias the estimates).
key_assumptions.supported_by: The national reading score in grade 8, measured after application but before the camp, and placebo tests on absence, socio-emotional skills and school well-being from grade 7 to grade 8 (Tables A.10-A.12) show no significant evidence of increased motivation.

implies_edges.to: pre-camp outcomes (grade 7-8 motivation, absence, school well-being, national test scores)

key_assumptions.assumption: The outcome measure is not contaminated by the graders: teachers' knowledge of who has participated in the program does not itself influence the marks they give.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Grade 9 school leaving exams graded by external censors (Figure A.3) and written exams that are completely independent of the teachers (Figure A.4) do not change the findings.

implies_edges.to: teachers' grading behaviour (measurement of the outcome)

implies_edges.to: a boy's own outcome

identification.source_of_variation: Participation in a two-week intensive learning summer camp with a one-year mentoring follow-up in the holiday between grades 8 and 9, compared before (grade 8) and after (grade 9) for participants and non-participants; the comparison group is reweighted by Entropy Balancing.

key_assumptions.assumption: Parallel trends: there can be no differential trends between the camp/mentoring and non-camp/mentoring groups in the absence of program participation.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Pre-program trends in the average assessment mark (Fig. 1 shows no difference in effect between December and June of grade 8); placebo test with a randomly selected synthetic 'camp/mentoring' group (Table A.9); a fake camp date in the summer holiday between grades 5 and 6 using national tests in reading and math (Table A.10); placebo tests on absence, socio-emotional skills and school well-being from grade 7 to grade 8 (Tables A.11-A.12).

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional parallel trends after reweighting: once the non-camp/mentoring group is reweighted by Entropy Balancing so that the covariate means are identical to the camp/mentoring group, the two groups' outcomes would have evolved in parallel; without it school performance is likely to develop differently with the underlying distribution of covariates.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Column 8 of Table A.1 shows that the means in the camp/mentoring and non-camp/mentoring groups are perfectly balanced across the full set of covariates; alternative balancing methods and propensity score matching (Table A.8) give similar estimates.

key_assumptions.assumption: The reweighted non-camp/mentoring comparison group has common support with the camp/mentoring group over the balanced covariates (positivity of the balancing weights).
No anticipation: the camp boys do not change their behaviour or performance before the camp in anticipation of participating (behaviour changes prior to summer camp could bias the estimates).
key_assumptions.supported_by: The national reading score in grade 8, measured after application but before the camp, and placebo tests on absence, socio-emotional skills and school well-being from grade 7 to grade 8 (Tables A.10-A.12) show no significant evidence of increased motivation.

implies_edges.to: pre-camp outcomes (grade 7-8 motivation, absence, school well-being, national test scores)

key_assumptions.assumption: The outcome measure is not contaminated by the graders: teachers' knowledge of who has participated in the program does not itself influence the marks they give.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Grade 9 school leaving exams graded by external censors (Figure A.3) and written exams that are completely independent of the teachers (Figure A.4) do not change the findings.

implies_edges.to: teachers' grading behaviour (measurement of the outcome)

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference: a boy's outcome does not depend on whether other boys participate in the camp/mentoring program (the non-participants are a clean comparison group).

implies_edges.to: a boy's own outcome

threats_discussed: Selection bias: camp/mentoring participating boys comprise a different population compared to the remaining population of boys who do not participate
Differential (non-parallel) trends in school performance between camp and non-camp boys
Camp boys being more motivated to change their behaviour before the camp than non-participants
Teachers grading the boys may be influenced by knowing who participated in the program
Camp boys changing their desired upper secondary education between grades 8 and 9, which lowers the bar for being assessed ready
Applying for the camp may be related to the limitations of the boy's local school
The positive effect might originate from the boys-only teaching rather than from the summer camp itself
robustness_checks: Gradually richer specifications, covariates and individual fixed effects (Table 1; Table A.2)
Entropy balancing on one, two and three moments and propensity score matching with 3, 5 and 10 neighbours (Table A.8)
Alternative comparison groups: boys from schools with camp participants enrolled and schools that never sent pupils to the camp (Table A.7)
Externally censored grade 9 school leaving exams and written exams instead of teacher assessment marks (Figures A.3 and A.4)
Placebo test with a randomly selected fake treatment group (Table A.9)
Fake camp date in the summer holiday between grades 5 and 6 using national tests in reading and math (Table A.10)
Placebo tests on absence, socio-emotional skills and school well-being from grade 7 to grade 8 (Tables A.11-A.12)
Test for effects on changing the desired upper secondary education (Table A.6)

value.as_printed: y_it = u_i + β0 + β1 Camp_i + β2 Time_i + δ_j (Camp_i ⋅ Time_i) + ϵ_it

index_sets.over: assessment time-points; Time_i is a time-period categorical variable containing two periods before and after camp/mentoring participation for the average assessment mark and one for the readiness assessment

value.normalisation: December in grade 8 is the reference time-point: the δ_j are the effects of camp/mentoring participation by time period relative to December in grade 8.

falsification.condition: Significant and large placebo effects would imply that the identification strategy does not capture systematically different trends in pre-program school performance between camp/mentoring and non-camp/mentoring boys; in the fake-treatment-group placebo, estimates different from zero indicate a violation of the identification strategy.
